forfeit|waive.distinction: You forfeit a right by losing it as a penalty, and waive it by giving it up voluntarily.

formidable|redoubtable.distinction: Formidable describes anything daunting to face, while redoubtable adds the respect an opponent has earned.

forswear|recant.distinction: To forswear something is to give it up on oath, while to recant is to withdraw a belief one once professed.

forswear|retract.distinction: To forswear is to renounce something solemnly for the future, while to retract is to take back what one has already said.

fortify|gird.distinction: To fortify a position is to strengthen its defences, while to gird oneself is to brace for what is coming.

fractious|nettlesome.distinction: A fractious child is irritable and quarrelsome, while a nettlesome problem is the thing causing the irritation.

fractious|peevish.distinction: Fractious behaviour quarrels and resists control, while peevish behaviour complains and sulks.

fractious|recalcitrant.distinction: Fractious describes someone quarrelsome and hard to manage, while recalcitrant describes someone who simply refuses to obey.

frugal|sparing.distinction: A frugal person spends little as a matter of principle, while a sparing one uses little of whatever is in question.

frugal|stinting.distinction: Frugal is praise for careful economy, while stinting is criticism for grudging what should be given freely.

frustrate|thwart.distinction: To frustrate an effort is to make it come to nothing, while to thwart one is to block it at a particular point.

furnish|render.distinction: To furnish something is to supply it, while to render is to cause something to become a certain way.

furtive|surreptitious.distinction: Furtive describes the guilty manner of someone hiding something, while surreptitious describes the secrecy of the act itself.

futile|vain.distinction: A futile effort achieves nothing, while vain can mean the same or describe a person too pleased with themselves.

gaffe|solecism.distinction: A gaffe is an embarrassing social blunder, while a solecism is a breach of correct usage or etiquette.

gambit|ploy.distinction: A gambit is an opening move that gives something up for position, while a ploy is any cunning tactic at any stage.

gambit|stratagem.distinction: A gambit opens a contest with a calculated sacrifice, while a stratagem is a scheme to outwit an opponent by deception.

garrulous|loquacious.distinction: Garrulous talk rambles on about trivia, while loquacious simply means talking a great deal.

gawky|ungainly.distinction: Gawky suggests the awkwardness of someone who has grown too fast, while ungainly describes clumsy movement generally.

gawk|lout.distinction: To gawk is to stare open-mouthed, while a lout is the crude and aggressive person who might be doing it.

gibe|jibe.distinction: A gibe is a mocking remark, while to jibe is for two accounts to agree; one insults, the other tallies.

gibe|scoff.distinction: A gibe is the taunting remark itself, while to scoff is to speak of something with derision.

glum|morose.distinction: Glum describes low spirits that show on the face, while morose adds a sullen and lasting gloom.

glum|saturnine.distinction: Glum is a passing gloom, while saturnine describes a temperament that is permanently dark and sardonic.

glum|sullen.distinction: Glum spirits are simply low, while sullen ones are low and resentfully silent about it.

grandiloquent|pompous.distinction: Grandiloquent describes inflated language, while pompous describes the inflated person using it.

grandiloquent|pontifical.distinction: Grandiloquent speech is swollen with grand words, while pontifical speech lays down opinions as though they were doctrine.

grandiloquent|portentous.distinction: Grandiloquent language is inflated in vocabulary, while portentous language is inflated with a false sense of significance.

gratis|gratuitous.distinction: Gratis means given free of charge, while gratuitous means given without any warrant at all.

gripe|grouse.distinction: To gripe and to grouse are both to complain; gripe suggests a nagging specific grievance, grouse a low general grumbling.

grisly|macabre.distinction: Grisly describes the gore of a scene, while macabre describes a fascination with death itself.

gusto|relish.distinction: Gusto is the vigorous enjoyment shown in doing something, while to relish is the act of enjoying it.

hackneyed|stock.distinction: A hackneyed phrase is worn out by repetition, while a stock character is standard equipment for the genre.

hackneyed|threadbare.distinction: Hackneyed describes a phrase used until it lost force, while threadbare suggests an argument worn through to nothing.

hackneyed|trite.distinction: Hackneyed stresses the overuse, while trite stresses the resulting staleness and lack of any freshness.

hamper|hinder.distinction: To hamper is to weigh something down so it moves badly, while to hinder is to get in its way.

hamper|impede.distinction: To hamper is to encumber with a burden, while to impede is to place an obstacle in the path.

haphazard|slapdash.distinction: Haphazard work has no plan behind it, while slapdash work has been rushed without care.

harangue|tirade.distinction: A harangue lectures an audience at length, while a tirade pours out anger at whoever is in front of the speaker.

harbinger|precursor.distinction: A harbinger announces what is coming, while a precursor is the earlier thing that led to what came after.

harbinger|predecessor.distinction: A harbinger is a sign that something is coming, while a predecessor is the person who held the post before you. One points forward, the other backward.

hardy|intrepid.distinction: Hardy is about surviving hard conditions, while intrepid is about walking into danger. A hardy plant endures the winter; an intrepid explorer chooses the ice.

hardy|stalwart.distinction: Hardy means tough enough to endure, while stalwart means loyal enough to be relied on. One is about constitution, the other about allegiance.

haughty|imperious.distinction: Haughty looks down on you, while imperious gives you orders. Haughty needs no power to be arrogant; imperious assumes it will be obeyed.

haughty|overbearing.distinction: Haughty holds itself above you in silence, while overbearing imposes on you actively. One is a posture, the other is pressure.

haughty|supercilious.distinction: Haughty is general arrogance of bearing, while supercilious is that arrogance showing in the face, especially the raised eyebrow and the faint sneer.

headstrong|willful.distinction: Headstrong means charging ahead against advice, while willful can also mean simply deliberate. A willful act was intended; a headstrong person will not be told.

heady|rash.distinction: Heady describes the intoxicating thing, while rash describes the person acting without thought. Heady success can make someone rash.

heretical|heterodox.distinction: Heretical implies a doctrine worth condemning, while heterodox merely notes it departs from the accepted line. Heretical carries the charge; heterodox carries the label.

hinder|impede.distinction: Hinder and impede both mean to slow progress, and are interchangeable in most sentences, though impede is the more formal and is preferred in technical writing.

hinder|stymie.distinction: Hinder slows progress down, while stymie stops it outright. A hindered plan is behind schedule; a stymied plan is going nowhere.

hodgepodge|melange.distinction: A hodgepodge is a confused jumble with no order to it, while a melange is a varied mixture that may be deliberate and attractive.

homogeneous|homogenous.distinction: Homogeneous is the standard spelling for uniform in composition; homogenous is a biological term about shared descent, now widely used as a variant spelling.

humble|humiliate.distinction: To humble someone is to lower their pride, which can be deserved and even good for them, while to humiliate is to shame them, which is a cruelty.

humble|mortify.distinction: Humble lowers someone's pride, while mortify makes them wish the ground would open. Mortify is the sharper, more personal of the two.

humdrum|prosaic.distinction: Humdrum is dull through repetition, while prosaic is dull through lacking imagination. A humdrum routine repeats; a prosaic description never lifts.

humiliate|mortify.distinction: Humiliate is what someone does to you, while mortify describes the burning shame you feel. You humiliate a rival; you are mortified by your own blunder.

hummock|knoll.distinction: A hummock is a small lumpy rise, often in marsh or ice, while a knoll is a smooth rounded hill in open country. Knoll is the gentler word.

imbue|permeate.distinction: Imbue needs an agent putting the quality in, while permeate describes something spreading through by itself. A teacher imbues students with curiosity; damp permeates a wall.

imbue|pervade.distinction: Imbue is what someone does to fill a thing with a quality, while pervade is what the quality itself does once it is everywhere in that thing.

immaculate|impeccable.distinction: Immaculate is about cleanness with no mark on it, while impeccable is about conduct or work with no fault in it. An immaculate shirt, impeccable manners.

imminent|impending.distinction: Imminent and impending both mean about to happen, but impending carries a sense of dread, so good news is imminent and doom is impending.

impair|mar.distinction: Impair damages how well something works, while mar damages how it looks or its perfection. A stroke impairs speech; a scratch mars a table.

impair|vitiate.distinction: Impair weakens something so it works less well, while vitiate spoils it so it no longer holds good at all. A false statement vitiates a claim rather than impairing it.

impecunious|penurious.distinction: Impecunious means simply having no money, while penurious can also mean mean with money. Only penurious can be an accusation about character.

impede|occlude.distinction: Impede slows any kind of progress, while occlude blocks a physical passage. Traffic impedes a journey; a clot occludes an artery.

imperil|jeopardize.distinction: Imperil and jeopardize both mean to put at risk and are interchangeable, though imperil is the more literary and jeopardize the commoner in ordinary prose.

imperious|overbearing.distinction: Imperious expects obedience as of right, while overbearing simply pushes until it gets its way. Imperious is colder; overbearing is heavier.

impertinent|impudent.distinction: Impertinent can also mean simply not relevant, while impudent is only ever about cheek. Impudent is the stronger word for disrespect.

impertinent|irreverent.distinction: Impertinent is cheek toward a person, while irreverent is disrespect toward what is held sacred. One offends a superior, the other offends the faithful.

impertinent|pert.distinction: Impertinent is genuinely offensive cheek, while pert is lively cheek that often charms. Pert is nearly affectionate; impertinent is a rebuke.

implacable|inexorable.distinction: Implacable means no appeal will soften it, while inexorable means nothing will stop its advance. An implacable enemy, an inexorable deadline.

implacable|relentless.distinction: Implacable is about refusing to be appeased, while relentless is about never easing off. A relentless rain is not angry; an implacable foe is.

implicit|tacit.distinction: Implicit means contained in what was said without being stated, while tacit means agreed in silence. A tacit agreement was reached; an implicit assumption was carried.

imposing|magisterial.distinction: Imposing impresses by sheer scale or presence, while magisterial impresses by authority and mastery. An imposing building, a magisterial history.

imposing|noble.distinction: Imposing is about the impression something makes, while noble is about its character or birth. A ruin can be imposing without being noble.

impregnable|inviolable.distinction: Impregnable means it cannot be taken by force, while inviolable means it must not be broken as a matter of principle. One resists attack, the other forbids it.

impregnable|unassailable.distinction: Impregnable is usually a place no attack can take, while unassailable is usually a position or argument no criticism can dent.

impudent|insolent.distinction: Impudent is brazen cheek, often from someone young, while insolent carries open contempt for the person addressed. Insolent is the colder offence.

inborn|innate.distinction: Inborn and innate both mean present from birth and are interchangeable, though innate is the word philosophy and psychology use for ideas and capacities.

incendiary|inflammatory.distinction: Incendiary can also mean literally setting fires, while inflammatory only ever inflames feeling. An incendiary device burns; inflammatory language enrages.

incessant|perpetual.distinction: Incessant stresses that it never pauses and usually irritates, while perpetual stresses that it never ends. Incessant noise annoys; perpetual motion continues.

incessant|unremitting.distinction: Incessant and unremitting both mean without a break, but unremitting suggests effort or pressure being kept up, so it suits work and rain more than chatter.

incipient|nascent.distinction: Incipient and nascent both mean just beginning, though nascent suits things being born into the world and incipient suits conditions starting to show.

incisive|keen.distinction: Incisive is only about cutting to the heart of a matter, while keen can also mean eager. A keen student may not be incisive.

incontrovertible|irrefutable.distinction: Incontrovertible and irrefutable both mean beyond dispute, though irrefutable answers an attempted refutation while incontrovertible forestalls one.

indecorous|unseemly.distinction: Indecorous and unseemly both mean improper for the occasion, though indecorous points at a breach of manners and unseemly at a breach of dignity.

indecorous|untoward.distinction: Indecorous is about behaviour that offends propriety, while untoward can simply mean unexpected and unwelcome. Nothing untoward happened is not about manners.

indigence|penury.distinction: Indigence and penury both name extreme poverty and are interchangeable, though penury is the older and more literary, and indigence the word legal and welfare texts use.

indolent|slothful.distinction: Indolent and slothful both mean lazy, but slothful carries the moral weight of the deadly sin while indolent is the cooler, more descriptive word.

inequity|iniquity.distinction: Inequity is unfairness, while iniquity is wickedness. An unequal pay scale is an inequity; a massacre is an iniquity.

inert|sluggish.distinction: Inert means not acting or reacting at all, while sluggish means moving but slowly. An inert gas does nothing; a sluggish river still flows.

inert|torpid.distinction: Inert describes something with no activity in it, while torpid describes a living thing gone dull and slow. A torpid animal will wake; an inert substance will not.

inexorable|intransigent.distinction: Inexorable means nothing will halt its advance, while intransigent means the person will not compromise. Processes are inexorable; negotiators are intransigent.

inexorable|relentless.distinction: Inexorable stresses that no plea will divert it, while relentless stresses that it never lets up. Both suit a glacier, but only inexorable suits a fate.

inexorable|stern.distinction: Inexorable means unstoppable and deaf to appeal, while stern means severe in manner. A stern judge may still relent; an inexorable process cannot.

inkling|intimation.distinction: An inkling is the faint sense you pick up, while an intimation is the hint someone else drops. You get an inkling; you are given an intimation.

insinuate|intimate.distinction: To insinuate is to hint at something damaging, while to intimate is simply to suggest indirectly. Insinuate always carries a sting; intimate need not.

insipid|vapid.distinction: Insipid comes from taste and suits food and art with no flavour, while vapid suits talk and expression with no thought behind it.

inspire|invigorate.distinction: Inspire puts an idea or impulse into someone, while invigorate puts energy into them. A speech can inspire a plan; a cold swim invigorates the body.
